title: Neurodegenerative Disease Pharmacology
summary: Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, Huntington's, MS and ALS drugs.

lessons.title: Parkinson Disease: Levodopa

levels.kid:
In **Parkinson disease**, a small group of brain cells that make **dopamine** slowly stop working. Dopamine helps the brain send smooth "move now" messages, so people get shaky hands, stiff muscles and slow movements.

Doctors can't just give dopamine, because it can't get through the brain's security wall. So they give **levodopa**, a building block that sneaks through the wall and gets turned into dopamine inside.

A helper medicine called **carbidopa** stops levodopa from turning into dopamine too early, out in the body. That way more reaches the brain and the tummy feels less sick.
levels.hs:
**Parkinson disease (PD)** happens when dopamine-making neurons in the **substantia nigra** die. These neurons send dopamine to the **striatum**, which helps start and scale movements. By the time symptoms appear, a large share of these neurons is already gone. Classic signs are **resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia** (slow movement) and later **postural instability**.

**Why not give dopamine?** Dopamine is charged and polar, so it cannot cross the **blood-brain barrier**. **Levodopa** (L-DOPA), dopamine's precursor, is carried across by an amino acid transporter. Inside the brain, the enzyme **DOPA decarboxylase** converts it to dopamine.

**Carbidopa** blocks DOPA decarboxylase **outside** the brain (it can't cross the barrier itself). That means:
- more levodopa reaches the brain
- less dopamine forms in the blood, so less nausea and low blood pressure

Levodopa–carbidopa is the **most effective** drug for PD symptoms. Over years, problems appear: the benefit wears off before the next dose (**wearing-off**), and patients can develop extra writhing movements called **dyskinesias**. Levodopa treats symptoms; it does **not** stop the disease from progressing.
levels.college:
**Pathophysiology.** PD involves loss of dopaminergic neurons in the **substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc)** with α-synuclein-containing **Lewy bodies**. Striatal dopamine loss shifts basal ganglia balance: reduced D1-mediated drive through the **direct pathway** and disinhibition of the D2-expressing **indirect pathway**, both increasing GPi/SNr inhibitory output to thalamus → hypokinesia.

**Levodopa pharmacokinetics.**
- Absorbed in the proximal small intestine by the **large neutral amino acid transporter (LAT1)**; dietary protein competes for uptake in gut and at the blood-brain barrier.
- Peripherally metabolized by **aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC)** and **COMT** (to 3-O-methyldopa).
- Short plasma half-life; erratic gastric emptying causes delayed or failed doses.

**Carbidopa** (or **benserazide**) inhibits peripheral AADC; **COMT inhibitors** (entacapone, opicapone) block the other peripheral route and prolong the levodopa response.

**Adverse effects:** nausea and vomiting (area postrema lies outside the barrier), orthostatic hypotension, hallucinations and confusion, sleepiness, and **motor complications**: wearing-off, unpredictable on-off, and **peak-dose dyskinesia**.

**Interactions:** nonselective **MAO inhibitors** can cause hypertensive crisis. **Dopamine antagonists** (typical antipsychotics, metoclopramide) worsen PD; for PD psychosis use pimavanserin, quetiapine or clozapine.

**Disease course:** the ELLDOPA and LEAP trials found levodopa neither speeds nor slows progression.

**Why symptoms appear late:** compensatory increases in dopamine turnover and receptor sensitivity in surviving terminals mask the loss until a large fraction of striatal dopamine is gone, so the disease begins years before diagnosis.
levels.phd:
**The short-duration problem.** Early in PD, surviving nigrostriatal terminals take up dopamine made from levodopa, store it in vesicles and release it physiologically, buffering fluctuating plasma levels (the long-duration response). As terminals are lost, conversion shifts to non-dopaminergic cells, notably **serotonergic raphe terminals**, which express AADC and VMAT2 but lack dopamine autoreceptors and the dopamine transporter. They release dopamine as an unregulated "false transmitter", producing large synaptic swings that track plasma levels.

**Pulsatile stimulation and dyskinesia.** Intermittent receptor stimulation in a denervated striatum drives maladaptive plasticity: D1 receptor supersensitivity, aberrant ERK and ΔFosB signaling in direct-pathway neurons, and loss of synaptic depotentiation. Peak-dose dyskinesia emerges from this primed state. Serotonergic lesions or 5-HT1A/1B agonists reduce dyskinesia in animal models, supporting the false-transmitter mechanism.

**Continuous delivery** follows from the theory: jejunal levodopa–carbidopa gel and subcutaneous foslevodopa–foscarbidopa (prodrugs cleaved by phosphatases) smooth plasma levels and reduce off time and dyskinesia.

**Non-motor biology.** PD is a multisystem synucleinopathy. Braak staging proposes caudal-to-rostral spread from the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and olfactory bulb; constipation, REM sleep behavior disorder and hyposmia may precede motor signs by years. Seed amplification assays now detect misfolded α-synuclein in CSF and skin. Levodopa does not treat these non-dopaminergic features, which explains much late disability: falls, dementia and autonomic failure.

**Genetics.** LRRK2 and GBA1 variants are the commonest genetic risk factors; LRRK2 kinase inhibitors and GCase-targeted approaches are in trials as possible disease modifiers.
levels.expert:
**Diagnosis first.** A clear, sustained levodopa response supports idiopathic PD. Poor response with early falls, early autonomic failure, vertical gaze palsy or symmetric onset suggests atypical parkinsonism (MSA, PSP). Before calling someone a nonresponder, check that the drug was actually absorbed and adequately trialed.

**Practical levodopa management:**
- **Protein redistribution:** advise taking levodopa away from protein-heavy meals if responses are erratic.
- **Gastric emptying:** delayed "on" often reflects gastroparesis or constipation; dispersible or non-oral options help.
- **Wearing-off:** add a COMT inhibitor, MAO-B inhibitor or dopamine agonist, or adjust the schedule. Inhaled or sublingual rescue options exist for sudden off periods.
- **Dyskinesia:** reduce peak exposure, add amantadine, or consider device therapy.

**Never stop levodopa abruptly** (for example, a patient kept nil by mouth in hospital). Abrupt withdrawal can cause **parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome**, resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome, with fever, rigidity, autonomic instability and rising CK. Hospital teams should give PD drugs on time and use a nasogastric route or a rotigotine patch when the patient cannot swallow.

**Drugs to avoid in hospital:** haloperidol, metoclopramide and prochlorperazine. For nausea use domperidone where available (watch QT) or other non-dopamine-blocking antiemetics; ondansetron is fine unless apomorphine is used. For delirium or psychosis, first reduce anticholinergics and amantadine, then agonists, then consider quetiapine, clozapine or pimavanserin.

**Neurosurgical angle:** a good levodopa response predicts benefit from **deep brain stimulation** of the STN or GPi, except for tremor, which can respond to DBS even when levodopa-resistant. Preoperative on/off testing quantifies this.

keyPoints: PD = loss of SNc dopamine neurons with α-synuclein Lewy bodies; tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability.
Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier via LAT1 and is decarboxylated to dopamine.
Carbidopa inhibits peripheral AADC, raising brain delivery and reducing nausea; it does not cross the barrier.
Motor complications: wearing-off, on-off and peak-dose dyskinesia.
Avoid D2 blockers (haloperidol, metoclopramide); never stop levodopa abruptly.
Levodopa is symptomatic, not disease-modifying (ELLDOPA, LEAP).

lessons.title: Other Antiparkinson Drugs

levels.kid:
Levodopa is the strongest Parkinson medicine, but there are helpers too.

Some medicines **pretend to be dopamine**. They press the same "go" buttons on brain cells. Others **slow down the cleanup crew** that breaks dopamine apart, so each bit of dopamine lasts longer.

There are also old medicines that calm a different brain chemical to help shaking.

Each helper has its own side effects, so doctors pick carefully. Some people later get a tiny brain "pacemaker" put in by a surgeon, which can calm the shaking a lot.
levels.hs:
Besides levodopa, PD drugs fall into a few groups:

**Dopamine agonists** (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine patch, apomorphine injection) directly stimulate dopamine receptors. They need no conversion and last longer than levodopa, causing fewer dyskinesias, but they are weaker. Side effects include sleepiness and sudden sleep attacks, swelling, hallucinations and **impulse control disorders** such as compulsive gambling, shopping or eating.

**MAO-B inhibitors** (selegiline, rasagiline, safinamide) block an enzyme that breaks down dopamine in the brain, making it last longer.

**COMT inhibitors** (entacapone, opicapone) block another breakdown enzyme mainly in the body, so each levodopa dose lasts longer. They are always used **with** levodopa.

**Amantadine** reduces levodopa-induced dyskinesia.

**Anticholinergics** (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) help tremor in younger patients but cause confusion, dry mouth and constipation, so they are avoided in older people.

When drugs aren't enough, **deep brain stimulation (DBS)**, an electrode placed by a neurosurgeon, can reduce off time, tremor and dyskinesia.
levels.college:
**Dopamine agonists.**
- **Non-ergot:** pramipexole and ropinirole (D2/D3-preferring), rotigotine (transdermal), apomorphine (D1 and D2; subcutaneous rescue for off periods, strongly emetogenic).
- **Ergot:** bromocriptine, cabergoline. Largely abandoned in PD because of **5-HT2B-mediated fibrosis** (valvular, pleural, retroperitoneal).
- Adverse effects: nausea, orthostasis, edema, somnolence and sleep attacks, hallucinations, **impulse control disorders** (strongly linked to D3 stimulation of the ventral striatum). Abrupt withdrawal can cause **dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome** (anxiety, dysphoria, pain).

**MAO-B inhibitors.** Selegiline and rasagiline are irreversible; safinamide is reversible and also modulates sodium channels and glutamate release. Selective MAO-B inhibition leaves gut MAO-A free, so dietary tyramine reactions are unlikely at usual use, though serotonergic interactions remain labeled.

**COMT inhibitors.** Entacapone and opicapone act peripherally; **tolcapone** also acts centrally but carries **hepatotoxicity** and needs liver monitoring. They extend levodopa half-life and reduce off time, and may increase dyskinesia; entacapone colors urine orange.

**Amantadine** blocks NMDA receptors, the most evidence-based oral antidyskinetic. Adverse effects: livedo reticularis, ankle edema, hallucinations; renally cleared.

**Anticholinergics:** striatal dopamine loss leaves cholinergic interneurons relatively overactive; muscarinic blockade helps tremor and dystonia.

**Istradefylline**, an **adenosine A2A antagonist**, reduces off time. A2A receptors are concentrated on indirect-pathway neurons, where they oppose D2 signaling.

**Device therapy:** DBS of STN or GPi, MRI-guided focused ultrasound for tremor, and continuous infusions.
levels.phd:
**Receptor subtype logic.** D1-like receptors (D1, D5) couple to Gs/olf and drive direct-pathway output; D2-like (D2, D3, D4) couple to Gi/o and inhibit indirect-pathway neurons. Pramipexole and ropinirole are D2/D3 agonists with highest affinity at **D3**, which is enriched in the nucleus accumbens and limbic striatum; this mesolimbic stimulation is the leading explanation for impulse control disorders, which occur in a substantial minority of agonist-treated patients and track exposure rather than disease severity. Apomorphine's full D1 and D2 agonism approaches levodopa efficacy, so it can reverse off states quickly.

**Why agonists dyskinesia less.** Longer half-lives provide more continuous receptor stimulation, and early agonist monotherapy delays dyskinesia onset. However, long-term trials (e.g., PD MED) show this advantage does not translate into better quality of life, because agonist side effects accumulate. Modern practice therefore favors levodopa whenever symptoms limit function, with agonists chosen case by case.

**Adenosine-dopamine heteromers.** A2A and D2 receptors form heteromers on indirect-pathway spiny projection neurons; A2A activation reduces D2 affinity and drives cAMP/PKA signaling. A2A antagonism therefore mimics dopamine on the indirect pathway, explaining istradefylline's benefit and the epidemiological link between caffeine intake and lower PD risk.

**MAO-B and neuroprotection.** MAO-B in glia oxidizes dopamine, generating hydrogen peroxide. The MPTP story showed MAO-B converts MPTP to the neurotoxin MPP+, taken up through DAT into complex I. This inspired neuroprotection trials (DATATOP, ADAGIO); the delayed-start ADAGIO design gave ambiguous results, so no agent is accepted as disease-modifying.

**DBS mechanisms** remain debated: high-frequency stimulation likely disrupts pathological beta-band synchrony in cortico-basal ganglia loops rather than simply lesioning. Adaptive closed-loop DBS uses local beta power as a biomarker to adjust stimulation in real time.
levels.expert:
**Choosing an add-on:**
- **Wearing-off:** COMT inhibitor, MAO-B inhibitor, agonist, or istradefylline; a rescue (apomorphine, inhaled or sublingual options) for sudden offs.
- **Dyskinesia:** reduce peak levodopa exposure, add amantadine, consider DBS.
- **Tremor-dominant young patient:** anticholinergic may help, but cognition must be watched; DBS or focused ultrasound for refractory tremor.
- **Older or cognitively impaired:** avoid anticholinergics and be cautious with agonists and amantadine (hallucinations, confusion).

**Screen for impulse control disorders** at every visit when patients take agonists. Patients often hide them; ask family. Management is dose reduction or switching to levodopa; taper slowly to avoid agonist withdrawal syndrome. Warn about **sleep attacks** before driving.

**Apomorphine pitfalls:** pretreat or cover nausea, but **do not combine with 5-HT3 antagonists like ondansetron**, because profound hypotension and syncope were reported.

**Serotonergic interactions:** MAO-B inhibitors carry labeled warnings with meperidine, tramadol, methadone and some antidepressants; meperidine is contraindicated.

**DBS selection (a neurosurgeon's view):**
- Good candidates: idiopathic PD, strong levodopa response (except tremor), disabling fluctuations or dyskinesia, preserved cognition, realistic goals.
- Poor candidates: atypical parkinsonism, dementia, severe untreated depression, axial symptoms (freezing, falls) that don't respond to levodopa.
- **STN** stimulation usually allows levodopa reduction; **GPi** directly suppresses dyskinesia and may suit patients with cognitive or mood vulnerability.
- Postoperatively, medications and stimulation are tuned together; abrupt dopaminergic reduction after STN DBS can unmask apathy or depression.

**Practical rule:** add one drug at a time and judge it against a clear target, such as hours of off time or dyskinesia severity, recorded in a symptom diary.

keyPoints: Dopamine agonists: pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine, apomorphine; risk sleep attacks and impulse control disorders.
Ergot agonists cause 5-HT2B-mediated valvular fibrosis.
MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline, safinamide) and COMT inhibitors (entacapone, opicapone, tolcapone) prolong dopamine/levodopa action.
Amantadine (NMDA antagonist) reduces levodopa-induced dyskinesia.
Anticholinergics help tremor but cause confusion; avoid in elderly.
DBS of STN or GPi for fluctuations, dyskinesia and tremor.

lessons.title: Alzheimer Disease Drugs

levels.kid:
**Alzheimer disease** makes people slowly forget things, like names, where they put their keys, and later even how to do everyday tasks.

Inside the brain, sticky clumps called **plaques** and twisty strings called **tangles** build up, and brain cells get sick.

Some medicines help brain cells talk better by keeping a memory chemical called **acetylcholine** around longer. Another one calms down a chemical that gets too noisy.

New medicines help the body's defenders clean up the sticky plaques. They can slow the forgetting a little, but they can't cure it yet.
levels.hs:
**Alzheimer disease (AD)** is the most common cause of dementia. Its brain changes are **amyloid plaques** (clumps of amyloid-beta outside neurons) and **neurofibrillary tangles** (twisted tau protein inside neurons). Neurons that make **acetylcholine**, important for memory and attention, are lost early.

**Cholinesterase inhibitors** (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) block the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine, so more stays in the synapse. They give modest improvement in memory and daily function for a while. Side effects: nausea, diarrhea, vivid dreams and a **slow heart rate**.

**Memantine** blocks **NMDA receptors**, which are overactivated by glutamate in AD. It is used in moderate to severe disease, often with a cholinesterase inhibitor.

**Anti-amyloid antibodies** (lecanemab, donanemab) are the first drugs that remove plaques and modestly slow decline in early AD. They require brain scans to confirm amyloid and MRI monitoring, because they can cause brain swelling or tiny bleeds (called **ARIA**).

None of these drugs cures AD. Avoiding drugs that block acetylcholine (some allergy and bladder medicines) is also important.
levels.college:
**Cholinergic hypothesis.** Degeneration of the **nucleus basalis of Meynert** reduces cortical acetylcholine, correlating with cognitive impairment.

**Cholinesterase inhibitors:**
- **Donepezil:** reversible, selective AChE inhibitor; long half-life.
- **Rivastigmine:** pseudo-irreversible carbamate inhibitor of AChE and **butyrylcholinesterase**; oral or transdermal; also approved for **Parkinson disease dementia**.
- **Galantamine:** reversible AChE inhibitor and allosteric potentiator of nicotinic receptors.
- Adverse effects: GI upset, weight loss, bradycardia, AV block and syncope (vagotonic), vivid dreams, urinary incontinence. Caution with β-blockers and conduction disease.

**Memantine:** low-affinity, **uncompetitive, voltage-dependent** NMDA channel blocker with fast off-rate. It preferentially blocks tonic, pathological extrasynaptic activation while sparing physiological signaling. Renally cleared.

**Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies:**
- **Lecanemab** binds soluble Aβ protofibrils; **donanemab** binds N-terminal pyroglutamate Aβ in established plaques, allowing treatment to stop once plaques clear.
- Phase 3 trials (CLARITY-AD, TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2) showed slowing of clinical decline by roughly a quarter to a third over about 18 months in early symptomatic AD with confirmed amyloid.
- **ARIA-E** (vasogenic edema/effusion) and **ARIA-H** (microhemorrhage, superficial siderosis). Risk is highest in **APOE ε4 homozygotes**; genotyping and serial MRI are required. Anticoagulation increases hemorrhage concern.
- Aducanumab's accelerated approval was controversial and the drug was discontinued.

**Behavioral symptoms:** antipsychotics carry a boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia; brexpiprazole is approved for AD agitation. Treat pain, infection and sleep problems first.
levels.phd:
**Amyloid cascade, revisited.** APP cleavage by β-secretase (BACE1) and γ-secretase (presenilin) generates Aβ peptides; Aβ42 is aggregation-prone. Familial AD mutations (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) and Down syndrome (APP triplication) support causality, while the protective Icelandic APP A673T variant reduces β-cleavage. Yet BACE inhibitors and γ-secretase inhibitors failed and some worsened cognition, likely from off-target substrates (Notch, other synaptic proteins) and treating too late.

**What antibodies teach.** Plaque removal with modest clinical benefit suggests amyloid is a necessary upstream trigger, but downstream **tau spreading**, microglial activation and synapse loss become partly autonomous. Donanemab's benefit was greatest in patients with low-to-intermediate tau PET, consistent with a therapeutic window before tau propagation dominates. Whether the effect size is clinically meaningful remains debated, given ARIA risk, infusion burden and functional-unblinding concerns.

**ARIA mechanism.** Antibody binding to vascular amyloid (cerebral amyloid angiopathy) triggers perivascular inflammation and complement activation, increasing vessel permeability (ARIA-E) and fragility (ARIA-H). APOE ε4 increases vascular amyloid burden, explaining the gene-dose relationship.

**Tau and beyond.** Tau propagates trans-synaptically in a prion-like manner along Braak stages; anti-tau antibodies and tau antisense oligonucleotides are in trials. Microglial genes (TREM2, CD33) from GWAS implicate innate immunity; TREM2-agonist antibodies are being tested.

**Biomarker revolution.** Plasma **p-tau217** approaches the accuracy of CSF and PET for detecting amyloid pathology, enabling cheaper screening. Revised biological definitions of AD based on biomarkers rather than symptoms are controversial, because many amyloid-positive older adults never develop dementia within their lifetime.

**Memantine pharmacology** illustrates kinetics as mechanism: its fast off-rate and voltage dependence let it leave the channel during strong synaptic depolarization, unlike high-affinity blockers that impair normal learning.
levels.expert:
**Making the diagnosis count.** Before prescribing, exclude reversible contributors: hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, depression, normal pressure hydrocephalus, subdural hematoma, medication effects (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, sedative antihistamines) and sleep apnea. For anti-amyloid therapy, confirm amyloid by PET, CSF or validated blood tests, and stage carefully (mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia only).

**Cholinesterase inhibitor practice:**
- Check pulse and ECG history; bradycardia, AV block and syncope are the serious risks, especially with β-blockers or digoxin.
- GI effects improve with slow titration or the rivastigmine patch.
- Stopping can cause noticeable decline; reassess benefit by function, not by test scores alone.
- **Prescribing cascade alert:** a cholinesterase inhibitor causing incontinence that is then treated with an anticholinergic bladder drug cancels the benefit.

**Anti-amyloid infusion programs:**
- Baseline MRI to exclude many microbleeds, prior lobar hemorrhage or superficial siderosis.
- APOE genotyping with counseling; ε4 homozygotes face the highest ARIA risk.
- Scheduled MRIs during the early months; most ARIA is asymptomatic but can cause headache, confusion, seizures, and rarely death.
- **Neurosurgical and stroke relevance:** patients on these antibodies should not receive thrombolysis without specialist input, because fatal hemorrhages have been reported. Ask about anti-amyloid therapy in any patient with AD presenting with stroke or a fall with head injury.

**Behavior:** nonpharmacological approaches first. Antipsychotics only for severe distress or danger, briefly, with mortality and stroke risk discussed. Avoid benzodiazepines. Treat depression with SSRIs cautiously (citalopram QT limits in elderly).

**Goals of care:** discuss driving, finances and advance directives early, while the patient can participate.

keyPoints: AD: extracellular amyloid-β plaques and intracellular tau tangles; early cholinergic loss.
Cholinesterase inhibitors: donepezil, rivastigmine (also BuChE, PD dementia), galantamine; watch bradycardia and syncope.
Memantine: low-affinity uncompetitive NMDA blocker with fast off-rate.
Lecanemab (protofibrils) and donanemab (plaque pyroglutamate Aβ) modestly slow early AD.
ARIA-E (edema) and ARIA-H (microbleeds) risk highest in APOE ε4 homozygotes; MRI monitoring.
Avoid anticholinergic drugs; antipsychotics carry a mortality warning in dementia.

lessons.title: Multiple Sclerosis Therapies

levels.kid:
Nerves are wrapped in a coating called **myelin**, like the plastic around a phone charger cable. It helps messages zoom along.

In **multiple sclerosis (MS)**, the body's own defenders, the immune cells, get confused and attack that coating in the brain and spinal cord. Then messages slow down, and people can get blurry vision, numbness or weak legs.

MS medicines calm down the confused defenders or stop them from getting into the brain. They help prevent new attacks. Other medicines help with tight muscles and tiredness.
levels.hs:
**Multiple sclerosis (MS)** is an autoimmune disease in which T cells and B cells attack **myelin** in the brain, optic nerves and spinal cord. Most people start with **relapsing-remitting MS**: attacks (relapses) such as optic neuritis, numbness or weakness, followed by recovery. Some later develop steady worsening (**progressive MS**).

**Treating a relapse:** a short course of **corticosteroids** speeds recovery. If that fails, **plasma exchange** can help.

**Disease-modifying therapies (DMTs)** reduce relapses and new MRI lesions:
- **Injections:** interferon-beta, glatiramer acetate (older, modest, very safe track record).
- **Pills:** teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate, and **S1P receptor modulators** like fingolimod, which trap lymphocytes in lymph nodes.
- **Infusions/antibodies:** **natalizumab** blocks immune cells from entering the brain; **ocrelizumab** and **ofatumumab** remove B cells; alemtuzumab wipes out many lymphocytes.

Stronger drugs work better but have bigger risks, such as infections. A serious brain infection called **PML** is the most feared.

**Symptom drugs:** baclofen or tizanidine for spasticity, and dalfampridine to improve walking speed.
levels.college:
**Pathogenesis:** autoreactive CD4+ Th1/Th17 and CD8+ T cells and **B cells** (antigen presentation, cytokines) cross the blood-brain barrier, causing inflammatory demyelination and axonal loss. Epstein–Barr virus infection is a strong epidemiological prerequisite.

**DMT mechanisms:**
- **Interferon-β:** reduces T-cell activation and MMP-mediated barrier breakdown. Flu-like symptoms, depression, liver enzyme rise.
- **Glatiramer acetate:** random polymer resembling myelin basic protein; shifts toward regulatory/Th2 responses. Injection-site lipoatrophy, transient post-injection reaction.
- **Teriflunomide:** inhibits **DHODH** (de novo pyrimidine synthesis) in proliferating lymphocytes. Hepatotoxic, **teratogenic** and very long-lived; elimination can be accelerated with cholestyramine.
- **Fumarates (dimethyl, diroximel):** activate **Nrf2** antioxidant pathways; flushing, GI upset, lymphopenia.
- **S1P modulators (fingolimod, siponimod, ozanimod, ponesimod):** functional antagonism causes S1P1 internalization, so lymphocytes cannot exit lymph nodes. First-dose **bradycardia** and AV block, macular edema, herpes infections. Siponimod needs **CYP2C9 genotyping**.
- **Cladribine:** deoxyadenosine analog resistant to adenosine deaminase; accumulates in lymphocytes (high dCK, low 5′-nucleotidase).
- **Natalizumab:** anti-**α4-integrin** antibody blocking VLA-4/VCAM-1 adhesion. **PML** risk rises with JC virus antibody positivity, longer treatment and prior immunosuppression.
- **Anti-CD20 (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, ublituximab):** deplete B cells; ocrelizumab is the first approved for **primary progressive MS**.
- **Alemtuzumab:** anti-CD52; profound lymphocyte depletion; secondary autoimmunity (thyroid, ITP, anti-GBM disease).

**Symptomatic:** **dalfampridine** (4-aminopyridine) blocks potassium channels exposed on demyelinated axons, improving conduction; it lowers seizure threshold.
levels.phd:
**Two diseases in one.** Relapses reflect focal adaptive-immune inflammation, which modern DMTs suppress very effectively. Disability, however, accrues mostly through **progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA)**, driven by compartmentalized CNS inflammation behind a relatively closed barrier: meningeal B-cell follicles, chronic active "smoldering" lesions with iron-rimmed microglia (paramagnetic rim lesions on susceptibility MRI), mitochondrial failure and axonal energy deficit. Peripheral immune drugs barely reach this compartment, explaining limited benefit in progressive MS.

**Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors** (tolebrutinib, evobrutinib, fenebrutinib) are CNS-penetrant and act on B cells and microglia. Results have been mixed across trials, with signals on disability progression in nonrelapsing secondary progressive MS alongside liver toxicity concerns, so their place is still being defined.

**Why B cells matter despite "T-cell disease" dogma.** Anti-CD20 therapy rapidly suppresses relapses without lowering antibody titers or plasma cells (which lack CD20). The effect therefore stems from removing B-cell antigen presentation and pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and B cells may present EBV-derived or myelin epitopes via molecular mimicry (EBNA1–GlialCAM cross-reactivity).

**Rebound biology.** Stopping natalizumab or S1P modulators can produce severe rebound disease activity, as sequestered or excluded lymphocytes flood the CNS, sometimes exceeding pretreatment activity. Switching strategies must minimize gaps.

**PML risk stratification** is a case study in pharmacoepidemiology: anti-JCV antibody index, duration beyond about two years and prior immunosuppressant use define risk strata; extended-interval dosing appears to reduce risk while preserving efficacy.

**Remyelination** strategies target oligodendrocyte precursor differentiation (e.g., clemastine's antimuscarinic effect on M1 receptors in the ReBUILD trial showed modest latency improvement), but no remyelinating drug is approved.
levels.expert:
**Is it MS?** Before committing to lifelong immunotherapy, exclude mimics. Most important: **neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD)** with **AQP4 antibodies** and **MOG antibody disease**. Interferon-β, fingolimod and natalizumab can worsen NMOSD, so test before treating severe optic neuritis or longitudinally extensive myelitis. Other mimics: vasculitis, sarcoidosis, B12 deficiency, small vessel disease.

**Choosing a DMT:**
- High-efficacy therapy early (anti-CD20, natalizumab) is increasingly favored for active disease, because early inflammation predicts long-term disability.
- Pregnancy planning shapes choice: teriflunomide and cladribine are teratogenic; natalizumab and S1P modulators carry rebound risk if stopped for pregnancy.
- Pre-treatment screening: hepatitis B (reactivation with anti-CD20), varicella immunity (S1P modulators), JCV serology (natalizumab), TB where relevant, and vaccination before B-cell depletion, since responses are blunted afterward.

**Monitoring essentials:**
- Natalizumab: JCV index; switch or extend dosing when risk rises; MRI surveillance for early asymptomatic PML.
- S1P modulators: first-dose cardiac observation for at-risk patients; eye exam for macular edema.
- Alemtuzumab: monthly blood and urine for years to detect ITP, thyroid and renal autoimmunity.
- Anti-CD20: immunoglobulin levels and infection history over time.

**Relapse management:** confirm a true relapse (new symptoms persisting beyond a day without fever or infection; heat and infection cause pseudo-relapses). Steroids hasten recovery but do not change long-term outcome.

**Neurosurgical relevance:** tumefactive demyelinating lesions can mimic tumors or abscesses, so consider MS before biopsy. Intrathecal baclofen pumps, placed surgically, treat severe spasticity, and abrupt pump failure causes dangerous baclofen withdrawal (fever, rigidity, seizures).

keyPoints: MS: autoimmune CNS demyelination involving T and B cells; relapsing or progressive.
Relapses: corticosteroids, then plasma exchange if refractory.
DMTs: interferon-β, glatiramer, teriflunomide (DHODH), fumarates (Nrf2), S1P modulators, cladribine, natalizumab (α4-integrin), anti-CD20, alemtuzumab (CD52).
Natalizumab → PML risk (JCV); S1P modulators → first-dose bradycardia and macular edema.
Ocrelizumab is approved for primary progressive MS.
Exclude NMOSD (AQP4) before starting interferon, fingolimod or natalizumab.

lessons.title: Huntington Disease and ALS

levels.kid:
**Huntington disease** is passed down in families. A gene has a stutter, a little piece repeated too many times. Over years it makes people's bodies dance and jerk without meaning to, and thinking gets harder. Medicines can calm the jerky dancing.

**ALS** is a disease where the nerve cells that tell muscles to move slowly stop working. Muscles get weak, and later talking, swallowing and breathing get hard.

A few medicines can slow ALS a little. A special new one can turn down a broken gene. Doctors, therapists and breathing machines help people live better and longer.
levels.hs:
**Huntington disease (HD)** is an **autosomal dominant** disease caused by an expanded **CAG repeat** in the **HTT** gene. The extra repeats make a toxic huntingtin protein that kills neurons, especially in the **striatum** (caudate). Symptoms: **chorea** (dance-like involuntary movements), psychiatric changes (depression, irritability) and dementia, usually starting in mid-adulthood.

**Treatment of chorea:** **VMAT2 inhibitors** (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, valbenazine) reduce dopamine packing into vesicles, so less dopamine is released. Important side effects: **depression and suicidality**, sleepiness and parkinsonism. Antipsychotics are an alternative. There is no drug yet that slows HD.

**Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)** destroys both **upper motor neurons** (brain) and **lower motor neurons** (spinal cord and brainstem). Patients get weakness, muscle wasting, twitching (fasciculations), stiffness and eventually breathing failure. Most cases are sporadic; about 1 in 10 are familial.

**ALS drugs:**
- **Riluzole** reduces glutamate excitotoxicity and modestly prolongs survival.
- **Edaravone** is an antioxidant that may slow functional decline in selected patients.
- **Tofersen** is an **antisense oligonucleotide** for ALS caused by **SOD1** mutations.

Breathing support (noninvasive ventilation) and feeding tubes improve survival and quality of life.
levels.college:
**Huntington disease pharmacology.** Medium spiny neurons of the **indirect pathway** degenerate first, disinhibiting the thalamus and producing chorea; later direct-pathway loss yields rigidity and bradykinesia.

**VMAT2 inhibitors** reversibly block vesicular monoamine transporter 2, depleting presynaptic dopamine (and to a lesser extent serotonin and noradrenaline).
- **Tetrabenazine:** metabolized by carbonyl reductase to dihydrotetrabenazine isomers, then by **CYP2D6**; genotyping guides higher exposure.
- **Deutetrabenazine:** deuterium substitution slows CYP2D6 metabolism (kinetic isotope effect), giving steadier levels and fewer peak effects.
- **Valbenazine:** prodrug of a single active (+)-α-dihydrotetrabenazine isomer, highly VMAT2-selective; approved for HD chorea and **tardive dyskinesia**.
- Warnings: depression and suicidality (boxed for HD), QT prolongation, parkinsonism, akathisia, sedation. Contraindicated with MAO inhibitors and reserpine.

**ALS pharmacology:**
- **Riluzole:** inhibits presynaptic glutamate release and persistent sodium current; extends survival by a few months. Monitor liver enzymes and neutrophils.
- **Edaravone:** free-radical scavenger; IV and oral formulations; benefit seen in an enriched early-disease population, not confirmed in a later oral trial.
- **Tofersen:** intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide that triggers RNase H degradation of SOD1 mRNA; lowers CSF SOD1 and plasma **neurofilament light**; accelerated approval for SOD1-ALS. Adverse effects include myelitis and aseptic meningitis.
- **Sodium phenylbutyrate–taurursodiol** was withdrawn after its phase 3 trial failed, a lesson in approving drugs on small phase 2 data.
levels.phd:
**HD: toxic gain of function and repeat instability.** Expanded CAG (polyglutamine) huntingtin misfolds, forms nuclear inclusions and disrupts transcription (sequestering CREB-binding protein), axonal transport, BDNF trafficking to striatum and mitochondrial function. Repeat length inversely correlates with onset age; paternal transmission favors expansion, producing **anticipation**. GWAS of onset modifiers identified **DNA mismatch repair genes** (MSH3, FAN1): **somatic CAG expansion** in striatal neurons over life may be the rate-limiting step, reframing HD as driven by ongoing repeat growth until a toxic threshold. MSH3 inhibition is now a therapeutic target.

**Huntingtin lowering.** Tominersen, a nonselective ASO, lowered CSF mutant huntingtin but phase 3 dosing was halted after worse outcomes in the higher-exposure arm, with signals that younger, lower-burden patients may benefit. Allele-selective ASOs (targeting SNPs linked to the expanded allele), AAV-delivered microRNA (AMT-130) and oral splicing modulators are in development.

**ALS: convergent proteostasis failure.** Around 97% of cases show cytoplasmic **TDP-43** aggregation with nuclear clearance, causing cryptic exon inclusion (e.g., in STMN2 and UNC13A transcripts). **C9orf72** hexanucleotide expansion, the commonest genetic cause and shared with frontotemporal dementia, acts by haploinsufficiency, RNA foci and dipeptide repeat proteins. SOD1-ALS is a notable exception lacking TDP-43 pathology, which may explain why tofersen succeeded biologically.

**Tofersen's regulatory lesson.** VALOR missed its primary clinical endpoint at 28 weeks, but neurofilament light fell markedly and open-label extension suggested slowing, especially with earlier start. Approval on a **biomarker reasonably likely to predict benefit** set a precedent for neurofilament as a surrogate. The ATLAS trial tests treatment of presymptomatic carriers once neurofilament rises.

**Excitotoxicity rationale** for riluzole: reduced astrocytic glutamate transporter EAAT2 in ALS motor cortex and spinal cord increases synaptic glutamate and calcium-permeable AMPA signaling in motor neurons.
levels.expert:
**Huntington disease in clinic:**
- Treat chorea only when it is disabling or causes falls or injury; many patients are less bothered than relatives.
- Before a VMAT2 inhibitor, **screen for depression and suicidality**, which are already common in HD; untreated depression is a contraindication. Review regularly.
- If psychosis, irritability or aggression coexist, an antipsychotic may treat both chorea and behavior.
- Check QT and interacting drugs (CYP2D6 inhibitors such as fluoxetine or paroxetine raise tetrabenazine exposure).
- Predictive genetic testing for at-risk relatives requires structured counseling; it is generally not done in minors for adult-onset disease.

**ALS in clinic:**
- Diagnosis uses clinical upper plus lower motor neuron signs and EMG (Gold Coast criteria). Exclude mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block (treatable with IVIG), cervical myelopathy, inclusion body myositis, Kennedy disease.
- **Offer genetic testing** to all patients now, since SOD1 status determines tofersen eligibility and C9orf72 matters for families.
- Start riluzole early; monitor liver tests.
- Multidisciplinary clinics improve survival. **Noninvasive ventilation** prolongs survival more than any drug; offer gastrostomy before respiratory function falls too low to make the procedure safe.
- Watch for respiratory depression from sedatives and opioids, but use them appropriately for breathlessness and distress in end-of-life care.

**Neurosurgery and HD/ALS:** DBS of GPi has been tried for severe HD chorea with variable results. For ALS, surgery's main roles are gastrostomy, tracheostomy and intrathecal access for ASOs; repeated lumbar punctures for tofersen sometimes need imaging guidance in patients with spinal deformity.

**Pitfall:** cervical spondylotic myelopathy can coexist with or mimic ALS; decompressing a spine in a patient with undiagnosed ALS will not halt progression.

keyPoints: HD: autosomal dominant CAG repeat in HTT; chorea, psychiatric change, dementia; striatal loss.
VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, valbenazine) reduce chorea; boxed depression/suicidality warning.
ALS: upper and lower motor neuron degeneration; TDP-43 pathology in most cases.
Riluzole (glutamate) modestly prolongs survival; edaravone is an antioxidant.
Tofersen: intrathecal ASO for SOD1-ALS, lowers neurofilament light.
Noninvasive ventilation and multidisciplinary care improve ALS survival.
